sections.title: How does the Exoplanet travel planner calculator work?
sections.html:
The Exoplanet travel planner calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports time passed on Earth (Space flight details) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the aim, the calculations mode and the destination); then you type in your age at start of trip, the engine efficiency (Space flight details), the required fuel mass1 and the maximum kinetic energy.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Exoplanet travel planner calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Time passed on Earth=(1 ÷ 299792458) × the square root of (distance × (spaceship acceleration × distance + 179751035747363528) ÷ spaceship acceleration)
Time passed on Earth=299792458 × (X1) ÷ spaceship acceleration
Spaceship acceleration=299792458 × X1 ÷ flight time
Time passed on Earth=(1 ÷ 299792458) × the square root of ((spaceship acceleration × distance + 89875517873681764 ^ 2) − 8077608713062490229263800746151696) ÷ spaceship acceleration
Time passed on Earth=299792458 × maximum velocity × the square root of (-1 ÷ ((maximum velocity ^ 2) − 89875517873681764)) ÷ spaceship acceleration
Maximum velocity=299792458 × β [v ÷ c]

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in light years
  • Time, opening in years
  • Time, opening in years
  • %, opening in percent
  • Mass, opening in metric tons
  • Energy, opening in 10²¹ of joules
  • Speed, opening in light speed
  • Energy, opening in megajoules

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Exoplanet travel planner calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — your age at start of trip, the engine efficiency and the required fuel mass1 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Exoplanet travel planner calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns time passed on Earth (Space flight details), derived from your age at start of trip, the engine efficiency and the required fuel mass1. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Exoplanet travel planner calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for your age at start of trip, the engine efficiency and the required fuel mass1, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter distance in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Distance opens in light years and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (6 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Distance = 4134325900000000000 ly. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Exoplanet travel planner calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
